groups.name: Caro-Kann
groups.intro: 1...c6 against 1.e4. A solid centre, a light-squared bishop that gets out before ...e6, and structures that repeat, so your plans transfer from game to game.

groups.name: Colle-Koltanowski

groups.name: Semi-Slav

openings.title: Lesson 1: The Setup & The e4 Break
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 ... 8.dxc5 Bxc5 9.e4
openings.idea: Master the core Colle-Koltanowski setup, the mandatory 8.dxc5 rule, and the thematic e4 central break.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 Nc6 6.Nbd2 Bd6 7.O-O O-O 8.dxc5 Bxc5 9.e4

3.e3.note: This modest pawn move is the whole opening. It opens the diagonal for your light-squared bishop.

4.Bd3.note: THE COLLE BISHOP. Look at where it points: straight at h7, next to Black's king. Almost every win in this opening ends with a sacrifice on that square.

5.c3.note: NOW we play c3, because Black attacks d4 and we need to defend it. GOLDEN RULE: play c3 only when Black plays ...c5.

6.Nbd2.note: Both knights are out. Notice the knight goes to d2, not c3 — it must not block the c-pawn.

8.dxc5.note: THE KEY MOVE OF THE WHOLE COURSE. Trade on c5 FIRST, then play e4. Black's pressure on d4 disappears, and his bishop lands on c5 where it does nothing.

9.e4.note: THE BREAK. Everything you did was preparation for this one move. The centre opens, your bishop on d3 comes alive, and the attack begins.

openings.title: Lesson 2: Classical Main Line vs 9...Qc7
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 ... 8.Re1 Qc7 9.e4 ... 13.Rh4
openings.idea: Handle Black's most critical response (9...Qc7) by executing the e4 central break, the thematic 12.Rxe4 rook recapture, and the 13.Rh4 rook lift attack.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 Nbd7 6.Nbd2 Bd6 7.O-O O-O 8.Re1 Qc7 9.e4 cxd4 10.cxd4 dxe4 11.Nxe4 Nxe4 12.Rxe4 Nf6 13.Rh4 Be7 14.Bf4 Qa5 15.Qc1 Rd8 16.Be5 Rd5 17.Qg5 Bd7 18.Rxh7 Bf8 19.Qh4

8.Re1.note: THE ROOK MOVE. Remember this: knight on d7 means Re1. The rook backs up the e-pawn and prepares for the coming central break and rook lift.

9...Qc7.note: Black's most natural move. He defends c7 and prevents you from playing e5 with tempo.

9.e4.note: THE BREAK. Open the centre and activate your pieces.

12.Rxe4.note: TAKE WITH THE ROOK. This is why Re1 was played. Recapturing with the rook gives you a powerful kingside attack, whereas taking with the bishop is quiet and dull.

13.Rh4.note: THE ROOK LIFT. Your rook swings sideways to the h-file and joins the attack on Black's king, aiming directly at h7 together with your bishop on d3.

18.Rxh7.note: The attack reaches its climax. White tears open Black's kingside cover for a decisive mating attack.

openings.title: Lesson 3: The ...Nbd7 Setup & The Rook Lift
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 ... 5...Nbd7 8.Re1 ... 12.Rxe4 13.Rh4
openings.idea: Learn how to adapt when Black plays ...Nbd7: switch from 8.dxc5 to 8.Re1, recapture with the rook on e4, and launch the devastating Rh4 rook lift attack.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 Nbd7 6.Nbd2 Bd6 7.O-O O-O 8.Re1 Qc7 9.e4 cxd4 10.cxd4 dxe4 11.Nxe4 Nxe4 12.Rxe4 Nf6 13.Rh4 Be7 14.Bf4 Qa5 15.Qc1 Rd8 16.Be5 Rd5 17.Qg5 Bd7 18.Rxh7 Bf8 19.Qh4

5...Nbd7.note: Black's other main setup. Because the knight on d7 overprotects c5, 8.dxc5 no longer works cleanly. You must switch plans completely to Re1.

8.Re1.note: THE ROOK MOVE. Memorize the rule: knight on c6 -> dxc5 then e4. Knight on d7 -> Re1 then e4. Getting this wrong is the most common mistake in the Colle.

12.Rxe4.note: TAKE WITH THE ROOK. This is why Re1 was played. Taking with the bishop is dull, but taking with the rook allows it to swing sideways to join the attack.

13.Rh4.note: THE ROOK LIFT. Your rook swings to the h-file and aims at h7 together with your bishop on d3. Black is already in grave danger.

18.Rxh7.note: The sacrifice arrives. Black's king cover is completely demolished.

openings.title: Lesson 4: Anti-Colle Diagnostics (Early ...Bg4 & ...Bf5)
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 Bg4 4.h3 Bh5 5.g4 Bg6 6.Ne5
openings.idea: Punish Black's attempt to solve his problem bishop early outside the pawn chain. Question the bishop immediately with 4.h3, 5.g4, and 6.Ne5 to secure the bishop pair and space advantage.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 Bg4 4.h3 Bh5 5.g4 Bg6 6.Ne5 Nfd7 7.Nxg6 hxg6 8.c4

3...Bg4.note: The anti-Colle. Black develops his bishop outside the pawn chain. Do NOT play 4.Bd3? on autopilot — Black gets a comfortable game with ...Nbd7 and ...e5.

4.h3.note: ASK THE QUESTION. Make the bishop decide right away. Simpler than 4.c4 and avoids gambit complications.

5.g4.note: Bold, but correct. The centre is closed, so flank advances carry no risk to your king while hunting the bishop.

6.Ne5.note: THE POINT. Plant the knight on e5, threatening to win the bishop pair or trap it with h4-h5.

7.Nxg6.note: Content yourself with the bishop pair. Do NOT play 7.h4?! because 7...Nxe5 8.dxe5 h5! overextends your kingside.

8.c4.note: Take the bishop pair and space advantage. Your plan: Nc3, Qb3 hitting b7/d5, and long-term positional pressure.

openings.title: Lesson 5: Queenside Fianchetto (4...b6) & Plan B: The Stonewall
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 ... 4...b6 5.O-O Bb7 6.Ne5 ... 11.g4
openings.idea: When Black plays 4...b6 and 5...Bb7 to blunt the e4 break, execute Plan B: build the Stonewall with 6.Ne5 and 8.f4, then launch a kingside pawn storm with 11.g4.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 b6 5.O-O Bb7 6.Ne5 Bd6 7.Nd2 O-O 8.f4 c5 9.c3 Ba6 10.Bxa6 Nxa6 11.g4 Qc7 12.g5 Ne8 13.Ndf3 g6 14.h4 Ng7 15.Ng4 h5 16.gxh6 Nf5

4...b6.note: The most testing way to meet the Colle. Black fights for control of e4 with a piece rather than a pawn, blunting your main break. When Plan A fails, switch to Plan B!

6.Ne5.note: PLAN B: THE STONEWALL. Put the knight on the strong e5-square and back it up with f4. Instead of breaking in the centre, you attack directly on the kingside.

8.f4.note: The Stonewall is built. Your pawn on f4 supports the knight and your rook can swing to f3.

10.Bxa6.note: TAKE IT HERE. Trading your bishop looks like a concession, but Black's knight is forced to the rim on a6 where it does nothing. Black spent two tempi just to end up with an offside knight.

11.g4.note: THE ATTACK. Push the g-pawn and open lines toward the black king. Throwing pawns at the king is simple and extremely effective at club level.

openings.title: Lesson 6: Punishing Passive Play (4...Be7)
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 ... 4...Be7 7.e4! ... 16.Bxh7+
openings.idea: Punish Black's passive move order when ...c5 is omitted: skip c3 entirely and execute an immediate e4 break, leading to a forcing kingside attack.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 Be7 5.O-O O-O 6.Nbd2 Nbd7 7.e4 dxe4 8.Nxe4 Nxe4 9.Bxe4 Nf6 10.Bd3 c5 11.dxc5 Bxc5 12.Bg5 Be7 13.Qe2 Qc7 14.Rad1 Rd8 15.Ne5 Bd7 16.Bxh7+ Kxh7 17.Bxf6 Bxf6 18.Qh5+ Kg8 19.Qxf7+ Kh7 20.Rd3

4...Be7.note: You will see this a lot at club level. Black develops sensibly but does not challenge your centre with ...c5.

7.e4.note: PUNISH IT IMMEDIATELY. Because Black never played ...c5, nothing attacks your d4-pawn, so you do not need c3 at all. No ...c5 from Black means no c3 from you — e4 comes for free!

10.Bd3.note: Retreat and keep aiming at h7. Your position is simply better: more space, better bishops, easier plan.

12.Bg5.note: Pin the knight. Now watch what happens when Black plays routinely.

16.Bxh7+.note: THERE IT IS AGAIN. Same sacrifice, different move order — proof that the h7-sacrifice pattern appears across the whole opening.

20.Rd3.note: White wins on the spot. The rook lift onto the h-file finishes the game with unstoppable mate.

openings.title: Lesson 7: The Phoenix Weapon (9.b4)
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 ... 8.dxc5 Bxc5 9.b4 Bd6 10.Bb2 e5
openings.idea: The positional alternative against prepared opponents: grab queenside space with 9.b4 (The Phoenix), expand with a3 and c4, and outplay Black in a reversed Semi-Slav structure.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 Nc6 6.Nbd2 Bd6 7.O-O O-O 8.dxc5 Bxc5 9.b4 Bd6 10.Bb2 e5 11.e4 dxe4 12.Nxe4 Nxe4 13.Bxe4 Be6 14.Re1 Rc8 15.a3 h6 16.Qe2 Re8 17.Rac1 Qc7 18.c4 Nd4 19.Bxd4 exd4 20.c5 Bf4 21.Rcd1 f5 22.Bc2 Bd5 23.Qd3 Bxf3 24.Qxf3

9.b4.note: THE PHOENIX. Instead of breaking in the centre with 9.e4, gain queenside space with tempo on the bishop. This reaches a Semi-Slav structure with reversed colours and a full tempo extra.

10.Bb2.note: Develop the dark-squared bishop immediately onto the long diagonal.

11.e4.note: Even in the 9.b4 lines, the central break eventually arrives — delayed by one move, but with your queenside territory already secured.

18.c4.note: THE PLAN ACHIEVED. Activate your queenside pawn majority with c3-c4 while restraining Black's kingside majority.

20.c5.note: The queenside majority rolls forward with decisive space, activity, and long-term positional pressure.

openings.title: Lesson 1: The Advance Variation — Core 3...c5 Break
openings.subtitle: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 ... 9.Nf5
openings.idea: Strike immediately at White's centre with 3...c5, get the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before playing ...e6, and target the d4-pawn via ...Nf5.
openings.pgn: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 cxd4 6.cxd4 Bg4 7.Be2 e6 8.O-O Nge7 9.Nc3 Nf5

3...c5.note: OUR MAIN WEAPON. We head for a French pawn structure without the bad bishop. We pay a tempo for a vastly superior light-squared bishop.

4.c3.note: White props up d4. Good news: this plays right into our hands, giving us a French structure with our bishop outside the pawn chain.

5...cxd4.note: THE SIMPLE ROUTE. We release the tension to get a clear, understandable position where d4 becomes White's permanent target.

6...Bg4.note: THE POINT OF THE VARIATION. Our bishop comes out BEFORE we play ...e6. In the French this bishop is Black's problem piece; here it is solved on move 6.

7...e6.note: Now we build the French structure. Our position is solid and every piece has an easy, natural square.

9...Nf5.note: THE KNIGHT'S HOME. On f5 it hits d4 and cannot be driven away by pawns without White wrecking his own king cover. Route: g8-e7-f5, never f6 where e5 kicks it.

openings.title: Lesson 2: The Advance Variation — 4.dxc5 (The Pawn Grab)
openings.subtitle: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.dxc5 Nc6 5.Bb5 e6
openings.idea: When White greedily grabs the pawn with 4.dxc5, do NOT chase it immediately. Develop with 4...Nc6, control the central light squares, and recover the pawn on your own terms while White falls behind in development.
openings.pgn: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.dxc5 Nc6 5.Bb5 e6 6.Be3 Ne7 7.c3 Bd7 8.Bxc6 Bxc6 9.Nf3 Nf5 10.Bd4 a5 11.O-O Nxd4 12.Qxd4 a4 13.Nbd2 Qa5

4.dxc5.note: White takes the pawn. This looks greedy, hoping we waste time chasing it or go passive. Develop first — the pawn usually returns on its own terms.

4...Nc6.note: DEVELOP, DO NOT CHASE. We hit e5 immediately and prepare to pick up c5 later. Two extra tempi are worth one pawn.

5...e6.note: We build the French structure now that the bishop can find a path out. Our knight will use e7 to head for the juicy f5-outpost.

6...Ne7.note: The correct square for the knight. On f6 it gets kicked by e5; from e7 it jumps to f5 to hit White's Be3 and d4.

9...Nf5.note: Our active piece placement bears fruit. The knight on f5 hits both Be3 and d4, while White's c5-pawn remains a target.

10...a5.note: A small but vital move: it permanently stops b4, which is White's only realistic way to hold on to the c5-pawn.

13...Qa5.note: Black regains the pawn with full equality, the bishop pair, and better piece activity.

openings.title: Lesson 3: The Advance Variation — 5.Be2 & The Bishop Manoeuvre
openings.subtitle: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Be2 Bf5 6.Nf3 e6 7.O-O Bg4
openings.idea: When White tries to nudge your bishop to f5 with 5.Be2, execute the brilliant two-step manoeuvre 5...Bf5 followed by 7...Bg4. Trading a tempo to guarantee trading off your bad bishop for White's key piece is a massive strategic victory.
openings.pgn: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Be2 Bf5 6.Nf3 e6 7.O-O Bg4 8.Nbd2 cxd4 9.cxd4 Nge7 10.h3 Bxf3 11.Bxf3 Nxd4

5.Be2.note: A clever move order by White, trying to force our bishop to remain on f5 where g4 ideas might hit it later.

5...Bf5.note: We develop the bishop anyway — setting up a deep strategic manoeuvre.

7...Bg4.note: THE PARADOX. We move the same piece twice! In closed positions, the QUALITY of development beats the SPEED of it. We guarantee trading our bad bishop and free f5 for our knight.

8...cxd4.note: THE TIMING POINT. We waited until White's knight committed to d2 before opening the c-file, so it can no longer recapture towards c3.

10...Bxf3.note: Trade off the bad bishop cleanly. If 10...Bh5 instead, White gets g4 and blocks our knight from reaching f5.

11...Nxd4.note: Black wins a key central pawn while keeping a dominant position.

openings.title: Lesson 4: The Classical / Tartakower Variation (5...exf6 Structure)
openings.subtitle: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6 6.Bd3 Bd6 ... 12.Qd7
openings.idea: Against White's Classical setup, accept doubled f-pawns with 5...exf6 for easy development, open files, and kingside attacking pressure via the ...Nf8-e6/g6 and ...Bxh3! battery.
openings.pgn: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nf6 5.Nxf6+ exf6 6.Bd3 Bd6 7.Nf3 O-O 8.O-O Re8 9.h3 Nd7 10.c4 Nf8 11.Be3 Be6 12.Rc1 Qd7 13.Qe2 Bxh3

3...dxe4.note: We offer the knight trade immediately to unbalance the structure and unburden our development.

5...exf6.note: RECAPTURE TOWARDS THE CENTRE. Do not take with the g-pawn. Our f6-pawn controls e5 and g5, denying White's knights an outpost.

8...Re8.note: ROOK FIRST, PIN LATER. By delaying ...Bg4 we tempt White into playing h3, creating a permanent weakness to target.

10...Nf8.note: THE REGROUPING. The knight defends h7/g6 and heads for e6 or g6 to support the attack.

12...Qd7.note: THE ATTACKING SCHEME. Queen and bishop both bear on h3. The permanent threat of ...Bxh3! completely paralyzes White.

13...Bxh3.note: THE KNOCKOUT SACRIFICE. Stripping White's king bare to launch an unstoppable attack.

openings.title: Lesson 5: The Panov-Botvinnik Attack (4.c4 & IQP Survival)
openings.subtitle: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e6 ... 13.bxc3
openings.idea: Master the two-phase strategy against White's Isolated Queen's Pawn (IQP): survive the middlegame without weakening your king, trade minor pieces safely, and target the weak d4-pawn in the endgame.
openings.pgn: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e6 6.Nf3 Bb4 7.Bd3 dxc4 8.Bxc4 O-O 9.O-O b6 10.Bg5 Bb7 11.Qd3 Nbd7 12.Rad1 Bxc3 13.bxc3 Qc7

4.c4.note: THE PANOV-BOTVINNIK. White attacks d4 immediately and accepts an isolated queen's pawn to claim active piece play.

6...Bb4.note: Pin the knight and add immediate pressure to the centre. Our strategy has two distinct phases: survive the middlegame, then exploit the isolated pawn in the endgame.

9...b6.note: Our standard setup: develop the bishop to b7 where it stares down the long diagonal at White's central control.

11...Nbd7.note: PHASE ONE: SURVIVE. Place the knight on d7 to cover e5 and f6 while avoiding premature central openings.

12...Bxc3.note: A concrete decision: hand over the bishop pair to permanently damage White's pawn structure and neutralize their grip on d5/e4.

13...Qc7.note: PHASE TWO: TARGET THE PAWN. With White's structure compromised, coordinate your rooks to pressure d4 and force an endgame where the isolated pawn is a fatal weakness.

openings.title: Lesson 6: The Exchange (4.Bd3) & The Fantasy Variation (3.f3)
openings.subtitle: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 Nc6 ... / 3.f3 e6 4.Nc3 Bb4
openings.idea: Neutralize White's quiet Exchange variation with active piece development, and handle the aggressive Fantasy variation (3.f3) by building a solid French-style structure with early pressure on the centre.
openings.pgn: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Nf6 6.Bf4 Bg4 7.Qb3 Qd7 8.Nd2 e6 9.Ngf3 Bd6 10.Bxd6 Qxd6 11.Qxb7 Rb8 12.Qa6 O-O 13.O-O Rb6 14.Qa3 Qxa3

4.Bd3.note: THE EXCHANGE VARIATION. Quiet and popular at club level. White releases the tension, resulting in a symmetrical, healthy structure.

6...Bg4.note: Bishop out before ...e6, exactly as everywhere else in this repertoire. We pin the knight and prepare to contest the centre.

7...Qd7.note: The cleanest answer: everything on b7 is defended and we keep our pawn structure completely intact.

3.f3.note: THE FANTASY VARIATION. Aggressive and popular with attacking players who want a big centre.

4...Bb4.note: Pin the knight and put immediate pressure on the centre. White's f3-pawn looks slow rather than strong.

6...O-O.note: Black is comfortable. White has spent a tempo on f3 that does not develop a piece, and we are better developed.

openings.title: Lesson 7: Anti-Caro Sidelines (Two Knights 2.Nc3 & King's Indian Attack 2.d3)
openings.subtitle: 1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 / 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 e5
openings.idea: Handle White's attempt to dodge normal Caro-Kann theory: pin the knight immediately with 3...Bg4 against the Two Knights, and aggressively seize the centre with 3...e5 against the King's Indian Attack setup.
openings.pgn: 1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.h3 Bxf3 5.Qxf3 e6 6.d3 Nd7 7.g3 Ngf6 8.Bg2 Bb4 9.Bd2 d4 10.Nb1 Bxd2+ 11.Nxd2

2.Nc3.note: THE TWO KNIGHTS. White develops flexibly to avoid main line theory.

3...Bg4.note: Our direct answer: pin the knight immediately and unbalance White's structure.

4...Bxf3.note: Take on f3. We hand over the bishop pair voluntarily, but White's structural integrity and control over e5 are compromised.

6...Nd7.note: Solid and flexible development, ensuring our pawn triangle on c6-d5-e6 neutralizes White's bishop pair.

2.d3.note: THE KING'S INDIAN ATTACK. White aims for a fixed setup regardless of what we play.

3...e5.note: GRAB THE CENTRE IMMEDIATELY. Do not wait passively; stake your claim in the middle before White can complete his setup.

openings.title: Lesson 1: The Modern Meran Main Line
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.e3 Nbd7 6.Bd3 dxc4 7.Bxc4 b5 8.Bd3 Bb7
openings.idea: Execute the Meran plan: take on c4 with tempo, expand on the queenside with ...b5, activate the light-squared bishop on b7, and strike in the centre with ...c5 to open lines for your pieces.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.e3 Nbd7 6.Bd3 dxc4 7.Bxc4 b5 8.Bd3 Bb7 9.O-O a6 10.e4 c5 11.d5 Qc7

3.Nf3.note: The standard move order leading to the Semi-Slav complex.

4...e6.note: THE SEMI-SLAV. Extremely solid, keeping both central (...c5) and queenside (...dxc4 followed by ...b5) breaks available.

6...dxc4.note: THE MERAN. Take on c4 with tempo on the d3-bishop, gaining time to expand immediately on the queenside.

8...Bb7.note: Our 'bad' bishop finally finds a powerful home on the long diagonal, staring directly at White's kingside.

9...a6.note: Supporting ...b5 so that the central break ...c5 comes with full force and preparation.

10...c5.note: THE CENTRAL BREAK. Everything played so far was preparation for this direct challenge to White's centre.

11...Qc7.note: Step off the d-file before it opens, eyeing e5 and keeping coordination flexible.

openings.title: Lesson 2: The Modern Anti-Meran (6.Qc2)
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.e3 Nbd7 6.Qc2 Bd6
openings.idea: Meet White's waiting move 6.Qc2 flexibly by developing with 6...Bd6, waiting for White to commit, and executing ...dxc4 only when the bishop must recapture, rendering White's queen misplaced on c2.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.e3 Nbd7 6.Qc2 Bd6 7.Bd3 O-O 8.O-O dxc4 9.Bxc4 b5 10.Bd3 Bb7

6.Qc2.note: THE ANTI-MERAN. A tricky waiting move intended to prepare b3 and force a pawn recapture after ...dxc4.

6...Bd6.note: We develop harmoniously and wait. Do not commit the centre prematurely when White is stalling.

8...dxc4.note: NOW we take, because the bishop must recapture. The whole point of White's queen on c2 evaporates instantly.

9...b5.note: Gaining queenside space with tempo on the c4-bishop, directly mirroring the main Meran setup.

10...Bb7.note: Our bishop settles on the long diagonal. White's queen on c2 is now awkwardly placed, facing down our coming rook on c8.

openings.title: Lesson 3: The Moscow Variation (5.Bg5 h6 6.Bxf6)
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.Bg5 h6 6.Bxf6 Qxf6
openings.idea: Neutralize White's immediate pin with 5...h6, accept the bishop trade on f6, and recapture with the queen to claim the permanent bishop pair and a clean, structural advantage with zero weaknesses.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.Bg5 h6 6.Bxf6 Qxf6 7.e3 Nd7 8.Bd3 dxc4 9.Bxc4 g6 10.O-O Bg7 11.e4 O-O

5...h6.note: ESSENTIAL REFLEX. Forces White to decide immediately and takes the ultra-sharp Botvinnik Variation permanently off the board.

6...Qxf6.note: RECAPTURE WITH THE QUEEN. We claim the permanent bishop pair and a healthy, completely uncompromised pawn structure.

9...g6.note: THE KEY STRATEGIC MOVE. Gives the queen a secure home on g7 and prepares ...Bg7, bringing our remaining bishop to life on the open diagonal.

10...Bg7.note: Complete the fianchetto. With White's dark-squared bishop already traded off, our g7-bishop has no counterpart on the board.

11...O-O.note: Castles safely into a pleasant, highly underrated position where our bishop pair gives us long-term winning chances.

openings.title: Lesson 4: The Meran Botvinnik System
openings.subtitle: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.Bg5 dxc4 6.e4 b5 7.e5 h6 8.Bh4 g5 9.Nxg5 hxg5 10.Bxg5 Nbd7
openings.idea: Enter the razor-sharp Botvinnik complexity, embrace the tactical chaos after White's piece sacrifice on g5, coordinate your minor pieces rapidly, and exploit White's exposed kingside.
openings.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 e6 5.Bg5 dxc4 6.e4 b5 7.e5 h6 8.Bh4 g5 9.Nxg5 hxg5 10.Bxg5 Nbd7 11.Qf3 Bb7

6.e4.note: THE BOTVINNIK INITIATION. White aggressively strikes in the centre right after our queenside expansion.

8...g5.note: THE COMPLICATION. We attack the pinning bishop immediately, provoking the legendary tactical explosion.

9...hxg5.note: Accept the temporary material imbalance. The position is a tactical battleground where our active pieces will shine.

think.title: The quiet queen move
think.brief: You're Black in the Caro-Kann. White just played 5.Qe2, a quiet move with a very loud idea.

stages.prompt: What did 5.Qe2 actually change?

options.text: The queen lines up with my king on the e-file, so my e7-pawn is pinned and no longer guards d6.
options.why: Exactly. e7 was the only piece covering d6, and now it can't move without exposing your king.

options.text: It prepares queenside castling and a pawn storm against my king.
options.why: Castling is a plan for later. Read what the move does right now: the queen is on the same file as your king.

options.text: It only defends the knight on e4 a second time.
options.why: It does defend e4, but that is the surface. The real change is behind your pieces, on the e-file.

stages.prompt: Tap the square White's knight wants to jump to.
stages.hint: Which squares can the e4-knight reach with check?
stages.explain: d6. Nd6 would be check, the only guard of d6 is the pinned e7-pawn, and your king is boxed in by its own pieces.

stages.prompt: Your natural developing move is 5...Ngf6. What is White's strongest reply to it?

options.text: 6.Nd6, and it is checkmate.
options.why: Checks first. d7 is blocked by your knight, e7 by the pinned pawn, d8 and f8 by your own pieces. Smothered.

options.text: 6.Nxf6+, a normal trade.
options.why: That's what you expect, not what White plays. Look at every check, not only the obvious one.

options.text: 6.Bg5, pinning the knight.
options.why: A decent developing move, but it misses the knockout. Checks, captures, attacks: in that order.

stages.prompt: Play the safe route. White's replies come automatically.

5...Ndf6.note: The d7-knight goes to f6. The d-file opens, so your queen now guards d6 as well: 6.Nd6+ would just lose a piece to ...Qxd6.

alt.e6: Also safe: the e-pawn steps off the pinned file.
alt.Qc7: Also safe: the queen covers d6 directly.

bad.Ngf6: 6.Nd6 is mate. The e7-pawn is pinned by the queen and your own knight on d7 blocks the king.

6...Nxf6.note: Recapture and you are out of the trap with a completely normal position.

7...Bg4.note: Pin the knight to the queen. White spent a tempo on Qe2 and achieved nothing.

debrief.t: 5.Qe2 put the queen on your king's file. That pinned e7, and e7 was the only guard of d6.
Your king had no free squares: d7, e7, d8 and f8 were all occupied by your own pieces.
Your opponent's CCAs matter as much as yours. Nd6 is a check, and after 5...Ngf6 it is mate.
5...Ndf6 opens the d-file so the queen guards d6. Calculate it: 6.Nd6+ Qxd6 and the trap is gone.

think.title: Remove the guard
think.brief: You are Black in the Advance with 3...c5. Everything you have done is aimed at d4. White just asked your bishop a question with 8.h3.

stages.prompt: What did 8.h3 do?

options.text: It attacks my bishop on g4, and does nothing for d4.
options.why: Right. A move that attacks one thing and defends nothing else gives you a free hand. Your bishop has to move or take, so make that move count.

options.text: It defends d4 a third time.
options.why: Look again: the h-pawn only touches g4. d4 has exactly the same defenders as before.

options.text: It prepares g4 and a kingside attack.
options.why: Your king isn't even castled. Read the concrete threat first: it's aimed at the bishop.

stages.prompt: Tap the pawn this whole position revolves around.
stages.hint: Your c5-pawn, your c6-knight and your b6-queen all point at the same square.
stages.explain: d4. You attack it three times (c5, Nc6, Qb6) and White defends it three times: c3, the f3-knight and the d1-queen. Remove one defender and it falls.

stages.prompt: Which CCA starts the win of d4?

options.text: 8...Bxf3, capturing a defender first.
options.why: Captures first, and the right capture: after Bxf3 the knight is gone and d4 has two defenders left against your three attackers.

options.text: 8...cxd4, taking on d4 straight away.
options.why: Your bishop is still hanging: 9.hxg4 and you've lost a piece. Deal with the attacked piece and the target in one move.

options.text: 8...Bh5, keeping the pin.
options.why: Solid but slow. White gets time for Be3 or dxc5 and d4 is safe again. The initiative was yours to take.

stages.prompt: Collect the pawn. Check White's counterplay at every step.

8...Bxf3.note: The guard is gone. d4 now has two defenders against three attackers.

9...cxd4.note: Now take. The c-file opens and d4 is about to fall.

10...Qxd4.note: The queen takes: centralised, and a clean pawn up.

bad.Nxd4: Natural, but 11.Bxd5! wins the pawn back: White has just enough activity. Take with the queen and the extra pawn stays.

11...Nxd4.note: A healthy extra pawn in the endgame, and the knight hits the f3-bishop. This is what pressure on d4 is for.

debrief.t: 8.h3 attacked the bishop and did nothing else. A one-job move gives you a free hand.
Advance structure: d4 is the base of White's pawn chain, the square your whole setup (...c5, ...Nc6, ...Qb6) is built to attack.
Count attackers and defenders: three against three. Capturing a defender with Bxf3 turns it into three against two.
Calculate to the end, including counterplay: 10...Nxd4? 11.Bxd5! hands the pawn back, while 10...Qxd4 keeps it.

think.title: One pawn, two targets
think.brief: You are White in the Colle. Black released the tension with ...c4 and just played 9...b5 on the queenside.

stages.prompt: What does 9...b5 tell you?

options.text: Black is busy on the queenside and did nothing about my e4-e5 push.
options.why: Exactly. Black's bishop on d6 and knight on f6 still stand on the two squares a pawn on e5 would attack.

options.text: Black threatens ...b4 to win my c3-pawn, so I must defend first.
options.why: ...b4 is a plan, not a threat that needs an answer this move. Check what your own pawn can do first.

options.text: Black is preparing ...e5 to take over the centre.
options.why: ...e5 isn't on the board yet, and your e-pawn gets there first.

stages.prompt: Tap the square where one pawn would attack two pieces.
stages.hint: A pawn on e5 attacks d6 and f6. What stands there?
stages.explain: e5. From there your pawn hits the d6-bishop and the f6-knight at once, and d4 protects it.

stages.prompt: Which CCA do you calculate first?

options.text: 10.e5, an attack on two pieces at once.
options.why: An attacking move that wins material by force. Black can only save one of the two pieces.

options.text: 10.exd5, a capture in the centre.
options.why: Captures are forcing, but this one wins nothing: 10...exd5 and the position is level.

options.text: 10.Qe2, developing and preparing Re1.
options.why: A good move in a normal position. Here it gives Black time for ...dxe4 or ...e5 and the fork disappears.

stages.prompt: Play the fork and collect the piece.

10.e5.note: The fork. d4 protects the pawn, so capturing on e5 only loses more material.

miss.Qe2: A sensible move in any other position, but e5 wins a piece right now.
miss.exd5: That releases the tension: after 10...exd5 the fork is gone for good.
miss.Re1: Too slow. The fork is available now and it will not come back.

11.exf6.note: Collect the knight. Black gets a pawn back with ...Nxf6 and you are a clean piece up.

debrief.t: 9...b5 was a queenside move. It didn't touch the centre and left the bishop and knight on the squares e5 attacks.
Colle structure: once Black plays ...c4 the tension is gone and e4-e5 gains space with tempo. d4 supports the pawn on e5.
Attacks count as CCAs: e5 hits two pieces at once, which is as forcing as a check.
Calculate Black's best try: 10...Be7 11.exf6 Nxf6 and you are a piece up for a pawn.

think.title: MSPC drill: the smothered mate
think.brief: You are a piece down. The entire MSPC cycle on one position: read the move, name the specifics, list the CCAs, then calculate to the end.

stages.prompt: What does Black's setup tell you?

options.text: The king on h8 has no escape squares: g7 and h7 are his own pawns
options.why: That is the feature the whole combination runs on. A king with no flight squares is a mating target, not a safe king.

options.text: Black is threatening ...Qxb2 and you must defend
options.why: Defending is exactly the reflex MSPC is built to stop. Read the position first: your attack is faster.

options.text: Black's extra piece means you should trade into an endgame
options.why: Trading when you are material down just loses more slowly. Look for the forcing line first.

stages.prompt: Tap the square both your queen and your knight can reach.
stages.hint: Your queen sits on the a2-g8 diagonal and your knight is on g5.
stages.explain: f7 is the intersection. The c4-queen covers it through d5 and e6, and the g5-knight jumps there with check.

stages.prompt: Which CCA do you calculate first?

options.text: Nf7+, because a check with the knight forces the king to a square you choose
options.why: Checks first. Forcing moves narrow the opponent's replies to almost nothing, which is what makes deep calculation possible.

options.text: Qxc6, because a capture wins material back
options.why: It wins a knight and loses the game to ...Qxb2 and counterplay. Checks come before captures when the king is boxed in.

options.text: Rd1, because an attacking move improves the worst piece
options.why: Slow moves come last. There is a forced mate on the board.

stages.prompt: Play the forced mate. Black's replies come automatically.

1.Nf7+.note: Check one. The king must go to g8 — the rook on e8 cannot capture and g7/h7 are blocked.

2.Nh6+.note: Double check from the knight and the queen together. Only the king may move, and 2...Kf8 runs into 3.Qf7 mate.

3.Qg8+.note: The queen sacrifice. It is not a sacrifice — it is a deflection: the rook is dragged onto g8 where it blocks the king's last square.

4.Nf7#.note: Philidor's Legacy. The king is smothered by his own pieces.

debrief.t: The king on h8 is walled in by g7 and h7 — no escape squares means mate patterns are live.
Your queen owns the a2-g8 diagonal, the knight has f7 and h6, and the black rook on e8 is one square from g8.
Checks, captures, attacks — and here the check is the move that keeps every reply forced.
Four moves, every one a check, so no calculation cutoff: at each step there was only one legal reply to consider.

think.title: MSPC drill: overloaded defender
think.brief: You are a bishop down and the black back rank is one move from collapse. Find the deflection.

stages.prompt: What has Black's play left behind?

options.text: Black never made luft: the king on g8 has no escape square.
options.why: That is the weakness everything else builds on. Three unmoved pawns in front of a king are a wall and a trap at the same time.

options.text: Black threatens ...Qd1+ with a back-rank mate of his own.
options.why: d1 is covered by your rook and your knight. Your back rank holds. The question is whether Black's does.

options.text: The bishop on b7 is loose, so I should attack it.
options.why: It is loose, but it is a slow target. Look for something forcing first.

stages.prompt: Tap Black's overloaded piece.
stages.hint: Which black piece is the only defender of the rook on e8?
stages.explain: The d8-queen is the sole defender of e8. An overloaded defender is the first thing to look for once you spot a weak back rank.

stages.prompt: Which forcing move do you check first?

options.text: Qxe8+, deflecting the queen onto e8
options.why: Take the defender's job away by force. After ...Qxe8 the queen is standing on the square she was defending.

options.text: Nd5, threatening to jump into e7
options.why: Black simply defends. A quiet threat gives the opponent a move; the back rank will be repaired with ...h6.

options.text: Re7, attacking along the seventh
options.why: The rook on e8 covers e7. Checks and captures come before attacking moves.

stages.prompt: Play it out.

1.Qxe8+.note: The queen is forced to recapture: the king cannot take, and no other black piece reaches e8.

2.Rxe8#.note: Back-rank mate. The pawns on f7, g7 and h7 that looked like a wall were the reason the king had nowhere to go.

debrief.t: Black never spent a move on ...h6, so the back rank has been a standing weakness the whole game.
One defender (the queen), one entry square (e8), one open file — that combination is what deflection tactics feed on.
Qxe8+ is both a check and a capture: the most forcing move available, so it is calculated first.
Two moves deep, but you must see to the end: the value of the queen is irrelevant once the line finishes in mate.

think.title: When Black forks first
think.brief: You’re White in your Colle-Koltanowski. After 10.Qe2, Black didn’t wait: 10...dxe4.

stages.prompt: What did 10...dxe4 change?

options.text: The pawn on e4 attacks my bishop on d3 and my knight on f3 at the same time.
options.why: Exactly. A pawn fork: unless you recapture, one of the two pieces is lost.

options.text: It only opens the d-file for Black’s rooks.
options.why: The d-file matters later. Right now that pawn attacks two of your pieces.

options.text: Nothing urgent. I can play Re1 first and take back later.
options.why: Then 11...exf3 wins a piece. Read what the move attacks before you follow your own plan.

stages.prompt: Apart from the king, only one black piece defends h7. Tap it.
stages.hint: Which black piece can reach h7 in one move?
stages.explain: The f6-knight. Trade it off and your Bd3 and Qe2 both point straight at h7.

stages.prompt: Which recapture keeps the advantage?

options.text: 11.Nxe4: it recaptures and offers to trade the f6-knight.
options.why: Right. After 11...Nxe4 your queen or bishop recaptures on the b1-h7 diagonal, aiming at h7.

options.text: 11.Bxe4: take back with the bishop.
options.why: 11...Nxe4 12.Nxe4 and your light-squared bishop is gone. The pressure on h7 disappears with it.

options.text: 11.Bc2: save the bishop first.
options.why: 11...exf3 wins the knight. A fork has to be answered with a capture or a check.

stages.prompt: Play it out. Black’s replies come automatically.

11.Nxe4.note: The capture that answers the fork and offers to trade Black’s best defender.

11...Nxe4.note: Black trades, and the f6-knight is gone.

12.Qxe4.note: Queen and bishop line up on h7. The threat is 13.Qxh7 mate.

alt.Bxe4: Also good: the bishop recaptures and keeps aiming at h7. The course line takes with the queen to force a concession.

12...f5.note: The only defence. 12...Bd7?? 13.Qxh7 is mate, and after 12...Re8 13.Qxh7+ White wins.

13.Qc4.note: The queen steps away from the f5-pawn and eyes e6 and the c5-bishop. After ...f5, e6 stays weak for the rest of the game.

alt.Qe2: Playable too. Qc4 keeps more pressure on e6 and c5.
alt.Qh4: Playable too, but Qc4 is more precise.

debrief.t: 10...dxe4 forked your bishop and knight. Read what the move attacks before you follow your own plan.
Only the f6-knight defended h7. Trading it turned your Bd3 and Qe2 into an attack.
Checks, captures, attacks: 11.Nxe4 is a capture that answers the fork and offers the trade.
After 12.Qxe4 Black had exactly one defence, 12...f5, and it left e6 weak for the rest of the game.

think.title: Attack first: the Meran ...b4
think.brief: You’re Black in your Meran. White skipped castling and pushed 9.e4 straight away.

stages.prompt: What did 9.e4 change?

options.text: White threatens e4-e5, kicking my f6-knight away from the centre.
options.why: Right. The pawn wants e5, and from there it hits your best defender.

options.text: It only builds a big centre. Nothing is threatened yet.
options.why: Read it as a threat: next move e4-e5 hits the f6-knight.

options.text: It prepares queenside castling.
options.why: Castling is far away. Look at what the pawn attacks next: e4-e5.

stages.prompt: Tap the square White’s pawn wants to reach next move.
stages.hint: Which square would attack your f6-knight?
stages.explain: e5. From there the pawn hits the f6-knight, and the c3-knight is what makes the push work.

stages.prompt: Which move meets the threat with a bigger threat?

options.text: 9...b4, attacking the c3-knight first.
options.why: Yes. If White ignores it with 10.e5, then 10...bxc3 11.exf6 cxb2 12.Bxb2 Bb4+ and Black comes out a pawn up.

options.text: 9...Qa5, pinning the c3-knight.
options.why: It looks active, but 10.O-O and e4-e5 still comes. The engine rates it far worse than 9...b4.

options.text: 9...e5, striking in the centre.
options.why: 10.dxe5 and the f6-knight is still in trouble. Deal with e4-e5 first.

stages.prompt: Play it out. White’s replies come automatically.

9...b4.note: Attack first. The c3-knight must move, and 10.e5? runs into 10...bxc3.

10.Na4.note: The knight goes to the rim. It no longer defends e4 or controls d5.

10...c5.note: The Meran break. d4 is attacked and the b7-bishop’s diagonal is about to open.

alt.Be7: Also playable, but ...c5 hits d4 right away.

11.e5.note: White pushes anyway and kicks the knight.

11...Nd5.note: The knight lands on d5, a central square no white pawn can ever attack: White has no c-pawn and the e-pawn has passed it.

alt.Bxf3: Also fine: 12.Qxf3 Nd5 reaches the same idea.

debrief.t: 9.e4 threatened e4-e5, kicking your f6-knight. Read the threat before you pick a plan.
e5 was the square that mattered, and the c3-knight was the piece that made it work.
9...b4 answered a threat with a bigger one: after 10.e5? bxc3 Black wins material.
After 10.Na4 c5 11.e5 Nd5 your knight owns d5, a square no white pawn can attack again.

clinic.title: The 5.Qe2 trap in the Caro-Kann

steps.t: 5.Qe2 looks slow, but it puts the queen on the e-file, straight at your king. Only the knight on e4 stands in between: the moment it jumps away, the queen looks through to e7 and e8.

Your king still stands on e8, and every square around it is taken by your own pieces: the queen on d8, the knight on d7, the bishop on f8 and the pawns on e7 and f7. A king without a free square can be mated by a single check.
White’s checks after 5...Ngf6: Nd6+. The only piece that could take on d6 is the pawn on e7, and it is pinned by the queen on e2. That check is mate.
5...Ngf6?? 6.Nd6# ends the game. 5...Ndf6 is the move: it challenges the knight on e4 and frees d7 for your king. After 6.Nf3 Nxe4 7.Qxe4 Nf6 you are fine.

clinic.lesson: Caro-Kann repertoire › Classical and the 5.Qe2 trap

clinic.title: The queen attack on f7

steps.t: 3.Qh5 attacks two things at once: the pawn on e5 and, together with the bishop on c4, the pawn on f7.
At the start of the game f7 is the weakest square in your camp: only your king defends it. Two white pieces now aim at it.
White’s captures if you ignore it: Qxf7 is checkmate, Qxe5+ wins a pawn with check, Bxf7+ is a check. The queen capture on f7 decides.
3...Nf6?? attacks the queen but ignores the threat: 4.Qxf7#. 3...g6 kicks the queen first, and after 4.Qf3 the knight goes to f6 and blocks the f-file. 3...Qe7 also defends f7.

clinic.lesson: Anti-Blunder Bootcamp › Read their threat first

steps.t: 5.Nxe5 leaves the queen on d1 hanging on purpose. The knight on e5 now attacks f7 together with the bishop on c4.
Your king is still on e8 and f7 is only defended by the king. The white knights on c3 and e5 are one jump away from d5 and f7.
White’s forcing moves after 5...Bxd1: Bxf7+ is a check, and after Ke7 the knight lands on d5 with mate. Before you take a free queen, list their checks.
5...Bxd1?? 6.Bxf7+ Ke7 7.Nd5#. 5...dxe5 is the least bad: after 6.Qxg4 you are a pawn down, but still in the game.

clinic.title: The Fishing Pole: don’t take the bait

steps.t: 5...h5 puts a pawn behind the knight on g4. If you take the knight, that pawn recaptures and the h-file opens toward your king.
You castled short, and the only thing that keeps the h-file closed is your own pawn on h3. The knight on g4 is bait on a fishing line.
Your capture: hxg4. After 6...hxg4 Black attacks your knight on f3, and the rook on h8 and the queen (via h4) aim straight at h2 and h1.
6.hxg4?? hxg4 and the attack comes fast: Stockfish gives Black close to three pawns. Leave the bait alone: 6.c3 prepares d4 in the centre and keeps White clearly better.

clinic.lesson: The MSPC System › C, Calculation: to the end

clinic.title: The Lasker trap: the knight promotion

steps.t: 5...dxe3 is not just a pawn capture. The pawn on e3 now attacks f2 and d2: next it takes on f2 with check.
Your king on e1 and your knight on g1 stand right behind f2. A pawn that takes on f2 with check can promote on g1 with check again.
Black’s forcing moves if you ignore the pawn: exf2+ and exd2+. Your own: Bxb4, fxe3 and Qa4+. Before you grab the bishop, look at their checks.
6.Bxb4?? exf2+ 7.Ke2 fxg1=N+! promotes to a knight with check, and Black wins material. 6.fxe3 removes the pawn: after 6...Qh4+ 7.g3 White holds.

clinic.lesson: The MSPC System › C, Calculation: to the end

bridge.title: The e3-e4 break
bridge.summary: Every piece in the Colle points at one pawn push.
plan: Trade first: dxc5 cleared d4 and pulled the bishop to c5, where your pawns can gain time on it later.
Break with e3-e4. The pawn arrives with the whole setup behind it: Bd3, Nbd2, Nf3 and the queen.
Follow up with e4-e5 when you can. It kicks the f6-knight, the one piece that defends h7.
bridge.mistake: Pushing e4 before the pieces are ready. If Black can take twice on e4, the trades kill your attack. Prepare it with dxc5, Qe2 or Re1.

drill.prompt: White to move. Play the break this setup was built for.

accept.e4: The Koltanowski break. Everything in the setup pointed at this square.

alt.b4: The Phoenix idea, 9.b4, gaining queenside space with tempo. The engine likes it even more, and it is covered in the advanced Colle lines.

bridge.title: Hit the base of the chain
bridge.summary: White grabs space. You attack its foundation.
plan: Strike the base straight away: ...c5 hits d4 before White has Nf3, c3 and Be2 in place.
Pile up on d4 with ...Nc6, ...Qb6 and ...Bg4, the bishop pinning the f3-knight that defends it.
If White overprotects d4, question the head of the chain later with ...f6.
bridge.mistake: Forgetting the c8-bishop. In the 4.c3 lines it comes out to g4 before ...e6. In the 4.dxc5 lines ...e6 comes first and the bishop stays home. Know which structure you are in.

drill.prompt: Black to move after 3.e5. Hit the base of the chain.

accept.c5: The move of this repertoire: you attack d4 before White can support it.

alt.Bf5: The classical 3...Bf5 is just as good. This repertoire uses 3...c5 to stay out of the sharp h4 and g4 lines.

bridge.title: Opposite-side castling
bridge.summary: Kings on opposite wings: centralise first, then break.
plan: White castled long and pushed h5, so the fight is on opposite wings.
Centralise first: ...Qd5 hits a2, controls e4 and e5 and supports the next break.
Then play ...c5 (and later ...b5) to open lines towards the white king.
bridge.mistake: Opening the kingside yourself with ...g6 or ...g5. The h5-pawn is there to punish exactly that.

drill.prompt: Black to move. Centralise before you break.

accept.Qd5: The queen lands in the centre, hits a2 and supports ...c5 next.

bad.c5: Too early. After 17. dxc5 Qc8 18. g4 White is clearly better. Centralise the queen first, then break.

bridge.title: The Meran ...c5 break
bridge.summary: Queenside space first, then the break that frees everything.
plan: ...dxc4 and ...b5 won queenside space and gave the c8-bishop the long diagonal via b7.
The break is ...c5: it hits d4 and opens the b7-bishop's diagonal towards White's king.
After ...c5 the knights head for c5 or b6 and the rooks go to the c- and d-files.
bridge.mistake: Waiting with ...h6 or ...Be7. White answers with e5 and d5 and your pieces get squeezed.

drill.prompt: Black to move after 10.e4. Play the Meran break.

accept.c5: The Meran break: it hits d4 and opens the b7-bishop's diagonal.

bad.h6: Too slow. After 11. e5 Ng8 12. Qe2 White is clearly better.

bridge.title: Moscow: bishops and the ...e5 break
bridge.summary: You gave up the centre for the bishop pair. Now open the diagonals.
plan: You gave White the centre and took the bishop pair in return.
The g7-bishop stares at d4. ...e5 (or ...c5) opens the long diagonal and frees your position.
Castle, then choose the break that fits: ...e5 when d4 is loose, ...c5 when White overextends.
bridge.mistake: Staying passive. Without a pawn break the bishop pair has no open lines to work with.

drill.prompt: Black to move. Open the long diagonal.

accept.e5: The central break: the g7-bishop comes alive and d4 is under fire.

alt.O-O: Castling first and breaking next move is also good.
alt.Qe7: Also good: the queen steps off the f-file and supports ...e5.

bridge.title: Anti-London: trade, then break
bridge.summary: The London's best bishop is gone. Your pawns do the rest.
plan: The trade on d3 removed the bishop that makes the London dangerous.
Your c6-d5-e6 pawns are solid. Free them with ...c5 or ...e5 once White commits.
Against c4, ...c5 and castling first are both healthy. White has no attacking target.
bridge.mistake: Playing for a kingside attack. With the light-squared bishops gone and your king safe, the game is decided by pawn breaks, not by ...g5 adventures.

drill.prompt: Black to move after 9.c4. Free your position.

accept.c5: The c-pawn break: it hits d4 while White is busy with c4.

alt.O-O: Castling first is just as healthy.

middlegame.title: The permanent hole
middlegame.brief: Black has traded the c-pawn and the light-squared bishop. Something in this position can never be defended by a pawn again.

stages.prompt: Tap the square Black can never cover with a pawn.
stages.hint: Black pawns sit on b5, d6 and e5. Which central square is out of reach of all of them, forever?
stages.explain: d5 is a hole. The c-pawn is gone and the e-pawn has passed it, so no black pawn will ever attack that square again.

stages.prompt: What is the plan?

options.text: Trade off the f6-knight, then park a knight on d5
options.why: Exactly. The f6-knight is the only piece still guarding d5. Remove it and a knight on d5 is untouchable.

options.text: Play f4 and exchange on e5 to open the f-file
options.why: That trades away Black's backward d6-pawn and frees the position. You are dissolving the weaknesses you want to attack.

options.text: Trade the dark-squared bishops with Bb6 or Bc5
options.why: The e7-bishop is Black's worst piece, boxed in by pawns on d6 and e5. Trading it does Black a favour.

debrief.t: Black's last moves gave up the c-pawn and the light-squared bishop — that is what created the hole.
Structure: pawns on d6 and e5 versus e4. d5 is a hole, d6 is backward on a half-open file.
No checks or captures win material here, so the priority is the positional one: control d5.
Calculate the trade sequence: any exchange on d5 must end with a white piece, not a white pawn, sitting there.

middlegame.title: Good knight, bad bishop
middlegame.brief: Material is level and there is one pair of rooks left. The imbalance is the minor pieces.

stages.prompt: Tap Black's worst piece.
stages.hint: Look at which colour squares Black's pawns are on, then find the piece that travels on those same squares.
stages.explain: The d7-bishop is bad: Black's own pawns on d5 and e6 stand on light squares and block every useful diagonal. The d4-knight, by contrast, can never be chased by a pawn.

stages.prompt: How do you convert that advantage?

options.text: Trade the rooks on c8 and head for the knight-versus-bishop ending
options.why: Right. Rxc8+ forces the trade, and with fewer pieces the bad bishop has nowhere to hide. Then the king walks to c5 or f6.

options.text: Play f5 to open the position
options.why: Opening lines gives the bishop air — after ...exf5 the d7-bishop suddenly has squares. Keep it locked.

options.text: Trade the knight for the bishop at the first chance
options.why: That removes the very piece the advantage rests on. You want the bishop to stay on the board, doing nothing.

debrief.t: The rooks face each other on the open c-file — whoever takes first decides whether pieces come off.
Fixed pawn chain on light squares, a knight that cannot be attacked by a pawn, a bishop that cannot get past its own pawns.
Captures first: Rxc8+ is forcing and improves the position, so it is the candidate to calculate.
Count the king race after the trade: Kf2-e3-d4 arrives before Black can create counterplay on the queenside.

middlegame.title: Blockade the isolani
middlegame.brief: You are Black. White has an isolated queen's pawn on d4: active pieces now, a permanent weakness later.

stages.prompt: Tap the square you want to occupy with a piece.
stages.hint: The square directly in front of an isolated pawn can never be attacked by a pawn.
stages.explain: d5 is the blockade square. A piece there is immune to pawn attacks, stops d4-d5 forever, and eyes both wings.

stages.prompt: What is your plan against the isolani?

options.text: Blockade d5, trade minor pieces, then attack d4
options.why: The standard recipe. Every trade makes White's attacking chances smaller and the weak pawn more important.

options.text: Play ...e5 straight away to hit the centre
options.why: After dxe5 the isolated pawn disappears and so does your long-term target. You have traded a permanent plus for nothing.

options.text: Storm the kingside with ...g5 and ...h5
options.why: The isolani side is the one that attacks. Opening your own king is exactly the game White wants.

debrief.t: White's setup — Bd3, Nf3, Nc3 — is aimed at the kingside. That is the price you accept for the weak pawn.
IQP structure: White gets e5 and d5 squares and open files; Black gets the d5 blockade square and a target on d4.
No forcing move yet. The priority is the blockade: ...Nb4 or ...Nd5 depending on how White defends.
Before every trade, calculate whether it leaves a blockader on d5 — if it does not, the trade helps White.

courses.middlegame.title: Free material: count before you move
courses.middlegame.idea: Most games under 800 are decided by one thing: a piece left undefended. Before every move, look at what your opponent just left hanging — and at what you are about to leave hanging yourself.
courses.middlegame.takeaway: Scan for undefended pieces every single move. Yours first, then theirs.

steps.prompt: White to play. Something is hanging — take it.

1.Nxd5.note: The queen stood on a square your knight attacks and nothing defended it. Free queen.

steps.prompt: White to play. A pawn can win a piece here.

1.axb4.note: Pawns capture too. The bishop stepped next to your a3-pawn with nothing defending it.

steps.prompt: White to play. Win material with check.

1.Qxd8#.note: You were counting a free rook — and it is mate, because Black never gave the king a square. Always look at what a capture does to the back rank.

courses.middlegame.title: The fork: one move, two targets
courses.middlegame.idea: A fork attacks two things at once, so the opponent can only save one. Knights fork best, but pawns do it too — and a fork with check is unanswerable.
courses.middlegame.takeaway: Look for squares where one piece touches two enemy pieces at the same time.

steps.prompt: White to play. Fork the king and queen.

1.Nf6+.note: Check and attack on the queen in one move. Black has to move the king, and the queen falls next.

2.Nxd5+.note: Collected. A knight that lands with check is worth calculating on every move.

steps.prompt: White to play. The knight has a fork square.

1.Nf7+.note: The classic f7 fork: king and rook at the same time, and the g7-pawn cannot take the knight.

2.Nxd8.note: A whole rook. Remember the shape — it repeats in hundreds of club games.

steps.prompt: White to play. A pawn move wins a piece.

1.e5.note: The pawn hits the bishop and the knight together, and d4 defends it. Black saves one piece, you take the other.

miss.d5: That attacks nothing. The fork was on the other side.

courses.middlegame.title: The back rank
courses.middlegame.idea: A castled king sits behind three pawns. That is shelter until a rook or queen reaches the back row — then it is a coffin. Learn to deliver it, and learn to give your own king a hole to breathe.
courses.middlegame.takeaway: Rook or queen on an open back rank plus three unmoved pawns equals mate. Give your king luft before it matters.

steps.prompt: White to play. Mate in one.

1.Ra8#.note: The pawns Black never moved are the reason there is no escape square.

steps.prompt: White to play. Black threatens mate on d1 — stop it.

1.h3.note: Luft. One pawn move and the back-rank mate is gone forever.

alt.g3: Also fine — the king gets g2. h3 is the usual choice because it keeps the g-pawn as a shield.
alt.f3: Playable, but it opens the a7-g1 diagonal towards your king. h3 is cleaner.
alt.Kf1: Also works: the king walks towards e2 and gets off the back rank. Luft with h3 is the habit to build.

2.Kh2.note: A check instead of mate. That is the whole difference one pawn move makes.

courses.middlegame.title: Pins and skewers
courses.middlegame.idea: A pinned piece cannot move without exposing something bigger behind it — so pile on and win it. A skewer is the same line the other way round: hit the big piece first and take what stands behind it.
courses.middlegame.takeaway: Line pieces — bishop, rook, queen — win material through other pieces, not around them.

steps.prompt: The e5-knight is pinned to its king and defended by the f6-pawn. Win it anyway.

1.d4.note: Attack the pinned piece with your cheapest attacker. The knight cannot run: moving it would expose the king to the rook.

bad.Rxe5+: The knight is defended by the f6-pawn: after ...fxe5 you have traded your rook for a knight.

2.dxe5.note: A pawn took a knight because the knight wasn't allowed to move. That is the whole point of a pin.

steps.prompt: White to play. Win the queen with a skewer.

1.Bb2+.note: Check on the long diagonal. The king must move, and it cannot take its queen with it.

2.Bxh8.note: Skewer: hit the valuable piece first, collect the one behind it.

courses.antiblunder.title: Read their threat first
courses.antiblunder.idea: Most blunders start before your own move: you didn’t read what your opponent’s last move wants. Before every move, ask one question: what does that move threaten next?
courses.antiblunder.takeaway: Their move first, your move second. Every single time.

steps.prompt: Black to play. White’s queen and bishop both aim at f7. Stop the mate, twice.

3...g6.note: The pawn chases the queen, and the queen was the piece threatening f7.

alt.Qe7: Also safe: the queen guards f7.
alt.Qf6: Also safe: the queen guards f7, though it can be chased later.
alt.Nh6: Also safe: the knight guards f7.

bad.Nf6: 4.Qxf7 is checkmate. The knight attacks the queen but leaves f7 with only the king to defend it.

4.Qf3.note: The queen comes back to f3 and aims at f7 again. Same target, new direction.

4...Nf6.note: The knight blocks the f-file and develops. Threat read twice, threat stopped twice.

alt.Nh6: Also holds f7, but f6 is the better square.

steps.prompt: Black to play. White’s knight just jumped to g5. What is it after?

endgame.title: Take the opposition
endgame.principle: Kings two squares apart on the same file, with the other side to move, is the opposition. The side that has it controls where the enemy king may go.

endgame.title: Rule of the square
endgame.principle: Draw a square from the pawn to the promotion rank. If the defending king can step inside it on his move, he catches the pawn without help.

endgame.title: Hold the draw with the opposition

endgame.title: Lucena: build the bridge
endgame.principle: With the king in front of the pawn and the enemy king cut off, the winning method is the bridge: rook to the fourth rank, king out, and interpose against the checks.
